items.title: Integration by parts is the product rule played backwards
items.claim: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u'v + uv'. Rearrange: uv' = d(uv)/dx - u'v. Integrate: integral of uv' dx = uv - integral of u'v dx. The formula isn't a separate tool — it's the product rule, integrated.

options.text: Choose u as the type higher in 'ILATE' priority: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. These tend to become simpler when differentiated; choosing them as u makes u'v easier to integrate than the original

items.reveal_title: Integration by parts and clever choices
items.reveal:
Integration by parts: integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du.

The formula always works mathematically, but the resulting integral can be HARDER than the original if you choose u and dv poorly. The ILATE heuristic helps:
- I: Inverse trig (arctan, arcsin)
- L: Logarithmic (ln x)
- A: Algebraic (polynomials)
- T: Trigonometric (sin, cos)
- E: Exponential (e^x)

Choose u as the FIRST function appearing in this list. Choose dv as the LAST.

Why: logarithmic and inverse trig functions become algebraic when differentiated; polynomials become lower-degree polynomials. Exponentials and most trig functions stay similar under differentiation, so we'd rather integrate them.

Classical applications:
- integral of x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx. Result: x e^x - e^x + C.
- integral of x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx. Result: -x cos x + sin x + C.
- integral of ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx. Result: x ln x - x + C.
- integral of x^2 e^x dx: apply twice.

Tabular integration (D-I tabular method) systematises repeated applications.

The Frullani integral, Bessel functions, and many special-function identities come from clever integration by parts. It's not just a textbook drill; it's the algebraic shadow of one of the deepest theorems in calculus (the fundamental theorem applied to product structures).
items.why: Integration by parts is taught as a mechanical technique. It's the product rule running backwards — and the ILATE heuristic is empirical wisdom about which functions are easier to differentiate than integrate.

items.title: There are true statements about numbers that cannot be proved
items.claim: Hilbert (1900) hoped to put mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic foundation. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved it impossible. Any system of axioms expressive enough to do basic arithmetic contains true statements that the system cannot prove.
items.prompt: What's the heart of Gödel's argument?

options.text: Gödel constructed a self-referential statement G: 'G cannot be proved within this system'. If the system could prove G, the system would prove something false (contradiction). If the system can't prove G, then G is true and unprovable

items.reveal:
Gödel encoded statements about mathematics AS numbers (Gödel numbering), so the system could 'talk about itself'. He then constructed a sentence asserting its own unprovability.

First incompleteness theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove.
Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself.

The results devastated Hilbert's program. They also bounded what computers can do: the halting problem (Turing 1936) is undecidable in essentially the same way.

Gödel was 25 when he proved it. Hilbert took it badly. Gödel later starved himself to death (1978) — convinced his food was being poisoned, he stopped eating when his wife was hospitalised.

Mathematics is still consistent (presumably), still useful, still extending — just provably incomplete.
items.why: Mathematics is treated as a closed, fully derivable system. Gödel showed any rich enough system has fundamental gaps — true things it can never prove.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.
